To mend something means to fix or repair it — to take something that is broken, torn, damaged, or not working properly, and bring it back to a good condition.

Think of a torn shirt. When you stitch it back together so it can be worn again, you have mended it. That is the heart of the word.

1. Repairing physical objects

This is the most straightforward use. You mend something that is damaged or broken.

  • She mended the hole in her jeans.
  • He mended the broken fence after the storm.
  • The cobbler mended my old shoes.

"Mend" in this sense is most commonly used for things like clothes, fabric, fences, nets, and similar items — things that can be patched, stitched, or put back together by hand. It feels more personal and hands-on than words like "repair" or "fix," which can be used for almost anything (machines, cars, buildings). You would say "mend a sock," but you would rarely say "mend an engine."

2. Healing the body

When a wound, a bone, or the body recovers from injury or illness, it mends. Here, no human action is required — nature does the work on its own.

  • The broken bone will mend in six weeks.
  • The cut on his hand mended quickly.
  • After the surgery, her body slowly began to mend.

This is a natural, gentle way to talk about physical healing. It suggests gradual recovery over time.

3. Repairing relationships and situations

"Mend" is also used for non-physical things — like a friendship that has been damaged, or a situation that has gone wrong.

  • They tried to mend their friendship after the argument.
  • It takes time to mend a broken trust.
  • The two countries worked hard to mend their relationship.

When you mend a relationship, you are taking steps to repair the damage — apologizing, communicating, being patient — just as you would stitch up a torn piece of cloth.

4. Correcting your own behaviour

"Mend" is used in the phrase "mend your ways", which means to improve your behaviour — to stop doing something wrong or harmful and start doing better.

  • His teacher warned him to mend his ways or face serious consequences.
  • She realised she needed to mend her ways and be more honest.

This usage is about self-improvement and correction. The idea is that just as you repair a damaged object, you can also repair your own flawed habits or behaviour.

This is one of the most common expressions using this word. "On the mend" means in the process of recovering or getting better — from an illness, an injury, or even a difficult situation.

  • He was very sick last week, but he's on the mend now.
  • Their relationship was tense for months, but it seems to be on the mend.

It suggests progress — things are not fully fixed yet, but they are moving in the right direction.
What Makes "Mend" Different from Similar Words

Fix and repair are the closest words in meaning, but there are subtle differences:

  • Fix is the most casual and broad. You can fix anything — a problem, a computer, a meal, a race. It does not carry the sense of careful, patient work.
  • Repair is more formal and is used for almost any kind of damage — cars, machines, buildings, electronics. It sounds more technical.
  • Mend sits between these two. It is warmer and more personal than "repair," and more careful and deliberate than "fix." It is especially suited to things that involve human care — stitching clothes, healing bodies, restoring relationships.

For example, you could technically "repair" a friendship, but "mend" a friendship sounds more heartfelt. The word carries a sense of tenderness and effort.

"Mend" is a quiet, gentle word. It does not suggest a quick or mechanical solution. It implies that something was hurt or broken, and that someone — or time itself — is patiently working to make it whole again. This is why it fits so naturally with relationships, emotions, and the body, and not just with objects.

In short, mend means:

  • To repair a physical thing (clothes, a fence) — usually by hand, carefully
  • To heal the body — naturally, over time
  • To repair a relationship or situation — through effort and care
  • To correct your own behaviour — through self-improvement
  • And in the phrase "on the mend" — to be in the process of getting better

The common thread across all these uses is the same: something was broken or damaged, and now it is being brought back toward wholeness.
